planting.note: Set out container-grown offsets or rooted rosettes in spring into sharply draining, gravelly or sandy soil; avoid winter planting in heavy soils where crown rot can set in before roots establish.

directions: Choose a site with fast-draining, rocky or sandy soil and full sun exposure that mimics the Mojave and Sonoran Desert slopes this species calls home. Established plants need no supplemental irrigation beyond occasional deep soaks during extended drought, and overwatering is the most common cause of failure. Clumps slowly form basal offsets that can be divided and transplanted to propagate new plants, and the stiff, narrow, curl-fibered leaves and tall creamy flower spikes make it a striking specimen or barrier planting. The fibrous leaves have a long history of use for cordage and soap by indigenous peoples of the region.

planting.note: Transplant container-grown rosettes in spring into well-drained caliche or sandy loam; give plants ample clearance from walkways since the rigid leaf tips are sharp.

directions: Plant in full sun on well-drained ground, ideally the caliche or sandy soils of the South Texas brushlands this species is native to. Over years it develops a stout, sometimes branching trunk topped with a dense rosette of rigid, blue-green, dagger-tipped leaves, eventually becoming a small tree. A tall panicle of white to cream bell-shaped flowers rises above the foliage in spring, drawing native yucca moths that are its exclusive pollinators. It tolerates heat, drought, and coastal salt exposure once established, making it a durable architectural anchor for South Texas and Gulf Coast xeric landscapes.

planting.note: Set out container plants in spring in rocky, alkaline, fast-draining soil; established sotols resent wet feet far more than cold, so drainage matters more than exact planting date.

directions: Site this Chihuahuan Desert native in full sun on gravelly, limestone-derived soil for best results, since it is markedly more cold-hardy than its Sonoran Desert relative Dasylirion wheeleri while sharing the same rounded rosette form. Leaves are narrower, smoother, and more blue-green than D. wheeleri, with fine marginal teeth that still warrant gloves during handling or division. Mature specimens send up a tall, wand-like flower stalk in summer that towers several feet above the foliage clump. It combines well with agave and cactus plantings in rock gardens and xeriscapes across west Texas and southern New Mexico.

planting.note: Transplant nursery-grown rosettes or pups in spring into rocky, well-drained soil on a slope or berm; avoid low spots where water collects around the base.

directions: Grow in full sun on a rocky, gravelly slope with excellent drainage, replicating the grassland-woodland transition zones of the Arizona and Sonora borderlands where this species grows wild. Broad gray-green leaves form an open rosette that, after years of slow growth, sends up a branched flowering stalk 10 feet or more in height whose nectar is a critical late-summer food source for migrating lesser long-nosed bats. Because it is monocarpic, the main rosette dies after flowering, but it typically leaves behind basal offsets that can be separated and replanted. Keep irrigation minimal once established, watering only during prolonged dry spells.

planting.note: Plant offsets or container stock in spring in gritty, fast-draining soil; in zone 8 areas provide a warm microclimate and winter protection from prolonged hard freezes.

directions: Plant in full sun to light shade in shallow, rocky soil, mimicking the central Arizona hillsides where this small, clump-forming agave is endemic. Unlike many of its larger relatives, it stays compact, spreading by stolons to form dense colonies of narrow, dark green leaves often marked with white leaf imprints and curling marginal fibers. It is an excellent choice for rock gardens or containers where a full-size agave would overwhelm the space. Water sparingly, since soggy soil is far more damaging to this species than the region's summer heat.

planting.note: Set out nursery-grown plants in spring into sharply draining, mineral cactus mix on a rocky slope; keep soil dry through the first winter to prevent rot while roots establish.

directions: Grow in full sun on a rocky, well-drained slope, ideally tucked among limestone or volcanic rubble as it occurs naturally in the sky-island grasslands of southeastern Arizona. Its densely packed, comb-like spines form distinct horizontal bands of white, pink, and reddish-brown that give the cylindrical stem its namesake banded, rainbow-like appearance even without flowers. In late spring, large magenta-pink funnel-shaped blooms open at the stem tips for several days, drawing native bees. Protect from overhead irrigation and standing water, which quickly leads to stem rot in this slow-growing species.
